flawed_step: Step 5: bridgeless cubic graphs need not have a 3-edge-colouring; the Petersen graph is a counterexample.
counterexample: Take the Petersen graph and replace one vertex by a triangle, attaching its three former incident edges to the three distinct triangle vertices. The resulting graph is finite, simple, cubic, bridgeless, contains a triangle, and is not 3-edge-colourable.
assessment_summary:
1. [JUSTIFIED] Let G be a finite simple bridgeless cubic graph containing a triangle T with vertices a,b,c.
2. [JUSTIFIED] Each of a,b,c has exactly one incident edge leaving T, since each already has two incident triangle edges and G is cubic.
3. [JUSTIFIED WITH CAVEAT] Contracting T produces a 3-regular incidence graph H; it may have parallel edges, so H need not be simple under the stated conventions.
4. [JUSTIFIED] H is bridgeless: a bridge of H would correspond to an external edge whose removal also disconnects G.
5. [NOT JUSTIFIED] The attempted proof asserts that H has a 3-edge-colouring merely because it is bridgeless and cubic. This implication is false; the Petersen graph is bridgeless, cubic, and not 3-edge-colourable. Moreover, H need not be simple.
6. [JUSTIFIED CONDITIONALLY] If H did have a proper 3-edge-colouring, its three edges incident with the contracted vertex would receive three distinct colours.
7. [JUSTIFIED CONDITIONALLY] Such a colouring lifts across T: if the external edges at a,b,c have colours 1,2,3 respectively, colour ab with 3, bc with 1, and ca with 2.
8. [NOT JUSTIFIED] Therefore concluding that every such G is 3-edge-colourable relies on the false Step 5.
9. [JUSTIFIED] To establish falsity explicitly, define the Petersen graph P with vertices u_i,v_i for i modulo 5 and edges u_i u_{i+1}, u_i v_i, and v_i v_{i+2}.
10. [JUSTIFIED] P is finite, simple, and cubic directly from this edge description.
11. [JUSTIFIED] P is bridgeless because every edge lies on a cycle: the outer edges lie on the u-vertex 5-cycle, the inner edges lie on the v-vertex 5-cycle, and each spoke u_i v_i lies on u_i-v_i-v_{i+2}-u_{i+2}-u_{i+1}-u_i.
12. [JUSTIFIED] In any 3-edge-colouring of a cubic graph, every colour class is a perfect matching, while the other two colours form alternating even cycles.
13. [JUSTIFIED] Every perfect matching of P contains either one or five spokes. The number k of spokes is odd because the 5-k unmatched vertices in each of the outer and inner 5-cycles must be paired internally. If k=3, the two vertices without spokes would need to be adjacent both in the outer cycle (index difference ±1) and in the inner cycle (index difference ±2), which is impossible modulo 5.
14. [JUSTIFIED] The complement of every perfect matching of P is two 5-cycles. For five spokes these are the outer and inner cycles. With one spoke, rotational symmetry permits taking u_0v_0; the forced remaining matching edges are u_1u_2,u_3u_4,v_2v_4,v_1v_3, whose complement consists of the cycles u_0-u_1-v_1-v_4-u_4-u_0 and u_2-u_3-v_3-v_0-v_2-u_2.
15. [JUSTIFIED] Hence P is not 3-edge-colourable: Step 12 would require the complement of a colour-class perfect matching to consist of even cycles, contradicting Step 14.
16. [JUSTIFIED] Form G* by deleting u_0, adding a triangle a,b,c, and replacing u_0u_1,u_0u_4,u_0v_0 by au_1,bu_4,cv_0 respectively.
17. [JUSTIFIED] G* is finite, simple, cubic, and contains the triangle abc.
18. [JUSTIFIED] G* is bridgeless. Triangle edges lie on the triangle; every other edge lies on a cycle obtained from a cycle of P by replacing any passage through u_0 with the corresponding path through the new triangle.
19. [JUSTIFIED] If G* had a 3-edge-colouring, its three edges leaving abc would have distinct colours, and contracting abc would therefore yield a proper 3-edge-colouring of P.
20. [JUSTIFIED] Step 19 contradicts Step 15, so G* is not 3-edge-colourable.
21. [JUSTIFIED] Thus G* satisfies every hypothesis and violates the conclusion, proving that the statement is false.
